Voyage log

    Reading the chart

    • The galaxy is ours, unchanged. Every named star, cloud and nebula sits where astronomers put it. Zoom in and the sea resolves into cells, each 20 light years across and one minute of sailing.
    • Colour is the sea's density as your crew feels it. Expanded, they sweep so much gas that it reads as a liquid: thin spray in hot bubbles, water in the open disk, thick water in the arms, reefs in molecular clouds. Reefs are impassable, so courses bend round them.
    • Thick water is rich and rough. Denser gas grows more prisms, prisms feed fauna, fauna grow bolder. Spray is safe and empty. A voyage is as hard as its roughest water or its destination, whichever is harder; two backers ease it one step.
    • Couriers are the only fast news. Every voyage shows how long light would take. A message the Ark carries in twenty minutes would take light four hundred years.
    • The side view is the disk edge-on, at true scale. The galaxy is 1,000 ly thick, 50 cells, so from far out it is a hairline; zoomed in, the gauge on the left shows where in that thickness your Ark is. Clouds are thin sheets near the midplane, and above and below the disk the sea thins to the halo's spray.
    • Courses keep to lanes by heading. Every course cruises at a height set by which way it heads: toward the centre, with the spin, out to the rim or against it. Courses that cross on the chart pass at different depths. With a voyage chosen, the side view is that voyage's profile: distance along the course across, height up, the sea sliced along the course, the eight lanes as dotted levels, and every lane it crosses marked at its own height with the depth between them.
    • Seven zoom tiers, from the whole galaxy to one star system. Sol and Tumult dive straight down; the ladder on the left jumps a tier. Each tier draws the stars that matter at that size, about a thousand on screen at any zoom. From Neighbourhood down, the chart shows a slice of the disk around one height, so nearby stars are not buried under the whole column.
    • Real stars near Sol, a model everywhere else. Within 1,600 ly of Sol the stars are the catalog's; past that, and behind the dust round Tumult, stars are drawn from the galaxy model, the same every visit. Near Tumult the brightest carry names Tumult's crews gave them. Tap any star or cluster to read it.
    • Crew's eye switches distances to what your expanded crew perceives: a cell is 2.25 million km, the whole galaxy 75 AU.

    The Milky Way, reimagined

    • Cell 20 ly; 1 minute per cell; Ark 20 ly a minute [S] Fact Sheet, Notion Timelines
    • Galaxy 100,000 × 1,000 ly; 80 hours across, 50 minutes through [S]
    • Heights from galactic latitude, with Sol 65 ly above the midplane; warm gas thins with a 360 ly scale height [D]
    • A course takes its planar cells or its climb in layers of foam-packed cells (0.82 of a cell each), whichever is more [D]
    • Perceived compression 8.4 × 10⁷, so perceived g/cm³ equals real atoms per cm³ [S] Garrett; [D]
    • Tumult to Sol about 24,000 ly, 20 hours [S] Timelines; placed here 23,900 ly from Sol, 2,300 ly from the centre [A]
    • Real positions from galactic longitude and distance; arms are a four-arm log spiral at 13° pitch with the Orion Spur; Sol 26,000 ly from the centre [D] standard astronomy
    • Stars within 1,600 ly of Sol: HYG v4.1 by David Nash / astronexus (Hipparcos, Yale, Gliese), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; this page's star table is adapted from it and shared under the same licence. Globular clusters: Harris 1996, 2010 edition (McMaster). Open clusters: Hunt & Reffert 2024, A&A 686, A42 (CDS VizieR) [S]
    • Every other star is drawn from the galaxy model: a disk falling off over 8,500 ly, the arms, the bulge and bar, and the local mix of bright and faint stars; about 9 stars per square ly at Sol, 30 times that near Tumult [M] model
    • Cloud and bubble densities are standard ISM values; their shapes here are simplified [D]
    • Lanes: eight headings, 40 ly apart, from 140 ly below the midplane to 140 ly above; a course climbs to its lane in its first 30% and down in its last 30%, never more than one layer of cells per cell, so the climb costs no time [A] proposed
    • Places near Tumult are invented (the slice's names first). Earth cannot see this region through the dust, so it is ours to fill [A]
    • Crew, factions and job words are the slice's voyage_slice.json [S]; hull, odds and rewards are this page's [A]

    Decisions for Garrett

    1. Tumult sits 2,300 ly from the galactic centre, toward Sol. Home waters are calm spray inside Tumult's own bubble; the centre's reefs are two hours out. Any point 24,000 ly from Sol fits the canon.
    2. The Heart (Sagittarius A*) is closed. The deepest well squeezes an infused traveller past return. The other option is a late lair.
    3. Sol is closed. The Terminal guards Earth's well, so courses route round it. The Hyades beacon is a proposed Terminal harbour for a start near Sol.
    4. Sea density sets danger and reward. Reefs over 100 g/cm³ are impassable.
    5. Sol to the edge. The map uses the real 26,000 ly from the centre; Timelines' 15 hours to the edge would need 32,000.
    6. Reefs are routed round, not over. They are sheets a few hundred ly thick, so a course could climb over one through thin water. Allowing it would add a slow, safe third course.
    7. Courses fly lanes by heading, like aircraft flight levels, so crossing traffic passes above or below. The open question is whether lanes are law (Terminal-kept, with pirates who break them) or just custom.
    8. Voyages run 8 to 55 minutes (160 to 1,100 ly), so the galaxy is a lifetime and Earth is a pilgrimage.

    Sources: HyperSea Fact Sheet, The Etherion Laws, Tumult World Model, HyperSea Charts (the earlier prototype), Docs/Voyages in the repo.
